englishSourceNotes: 'My favorite clothes' is plural but the child circles ONE picture; 'My favorite piece of clothing' or 'My favorite thing to wear' fits the task. French uses the singular 'Mon vêtement préféré'.

'My favorite breakfast' offers single items (juice, sausage, croissant), not whole breakfasts. Acceptable, but 'My favorite breakfast food' is more exact. French keeps 'Mon petit-déjeuner préféré' (26 chars, over the 22 target; it wraps to 2 lines).
'My favorite bug' includes snail, spider and worm, which are not insects. Informal English tolerates it; French 'petite bête' (the maternelle term) is exactly right for this set.

'My favorite pet' includes frog and parrot. Fine, but note the 'pet' set on copy 2 and the 'animal' heading on copy 1 are different sheets, so French 'Mon petit animal préféré' does not collide on one page.
'I can help tidy up' is cued by a BROOM, which a child reads as sweeping. Either change the cue (e.g. toys/bucket or a toy box) or the sentence to 'I can sweep the floor'.
'I can walk a long way' is cued by a hiker with a backpack and poles; OK, though 'I can go on a hike' matches the picture more directly.
'I can play a board game' is cued by a single die; acceptable.

optionWordFlags.problem: 'poulet' is the meat/food word; a live farm hen is 'poule' for a French child. Wrong register on a farm-animal row.
The picture is a thick American pancake stack with butter; a French child knows a crêpe as thin and flat. Mismatch between word and picture ('pancake' would be the accurate loanword).
Same picture as breakfast/pancake (thick stack), labelled crêpe. Mismatch.
The picture is a plain untoasted slice of sandwich bread; 'toast' is understood in France but the image reads as 'pain de mie'. Minor.
Copy 3 prints the hobby row and the vehicle row on the same sheet; vehicles/bicycle is also 'vélo', so the same word can appear twice on one page.
Correct, but children say 'flamant rose'; bare 'flamant' may not be recognised. Minor.

otherNotes: All sentences are gender-neutral (no 'tout seul/toute seule', no participles), so no agreement with the child's gender is needed.

Register follows the shipped 'can' list: mostly present tense 'Je …', 'Je sais …' where the skill is a learned competence (me peigner, m'habiller, coller). Longest sentence: 'Je fais voler un cerf-volant' (28).
'hobby' uses 'activité' rather than 'loisir': 'activité' is the word used in maternelle; 'loisir' is adult register.
'treat' uses 'gourmandise' (covers lollipop, cake and waffle); 'dessert' would wrongly exclude sucette.

Over the 22-char heading target: 'Mon petit animal préféré' (24), 'Ma gourmandise préférée' (23), 'Ma petite bête préférée' (23), 'Mon animal marin préféré' (24), 'Mon petit-déjeuner préféré' (26), 'Mon animal de ferme préféré' (27). All break cleanly onto 2 lines; no shorter natural French keeps 'préféré'. If a hard 22 is required: pet → 'Mon animal familier', farm → 'Mon animal de la ferme' (both drop 'préféré').
'backpack' → 'cartable': the word a French child uses for the school bag, including backpack-style ones; 'sac à dos' reads as a hiking bag.
Follow-up: tidy/coat/swing/draw revised to match the US panel. swing uses 'sans aide' to avoid gendered 'tout seul/toute seule'. bake kept: 'J'aide à faire un gâteau' still fits a whisk cue.
